text: But when the war broke out that August, Michael, who had been a sergeant in his schools Officers Training Corps, wanted to enlist at once as an ordinary soldier. <break time="0.8s" /> Instead, he was persuaded to accept a commission in a battalion so new that some of its men still wore old red uniforms, and so he became a lieutenant. <break time="0.8s" /> For months the battalion guarded the English coast and a Scottish estuary, and not until later was it sent to France, where it moved from one sector to another before reaching Ypres. <break time="0.8s" /> Michael wrote home that there was nothing special going on, but about a month later a fragment of a shell, falling out of a wet dawn, killed him instantly. <break time="0.8s" /> The next shell buried his body beneath the ruined foundations of a barn wall, and for a long time no trace of him could be found. <break time="0.8s" /> When the telegram announced that Michael was missing, Helen told herself that missing always means dead, and the inquiries she made through various organizations brought her no news. <break time="0.8s" /> In the months that followed she felt strangely numb, as if life were going on somewhere far away, and even the Armistice, which ended the war, passed over her unnoticed. <break time="0.8s" /> At last she was officially informed that his body had been found, identified, and buried again in Hagenzeele Third Military Cemetery, and she received his identity disc and watch.
